case_name: Scotford Electrical et al v. Blue Mountain Log Sales et al
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Scotford Electrical et al v. Blue
Mountain Log Sales et al,

2005 BCSC 538

Date: 20050412

Docket:
S0014008

Registry: Chilliwack

Between:

Scotford Electrical & Technical
Services Ltd.

Plaintiff

And

Blue Mountain Log Sales Ltd., doing
business as North American Wood Treating, Rae Fujikawa

Defendants

Before:
Master Groves

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

R.
J. Gantzert

Counsel for the Defendant, Blue Mountain
Log Sales Ltd.:

J.
G. Dives

Date and
Place of Hearing:

February 24, 2005

New Westminster, B.C.

I.          INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This action involves a claim by Scotford
Electrical & Technical Services Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as
“Scotford”) for unpaid accounts for goods and services for work performed on a
planer mill developed by the defendant Blue Mountain Log Sales Ltd.
(hereinafter referred to as “Blue Mountain”) in Abbotsford.  The plaintiff
initially filed a lien and later issued a writ of summons and statement of
claim to collect the outstanding amount.  Blue Mountain has counter-claimed for
breach of contract, negligence, negligent misrepresentation and wrongful filing
of a lien.  The claim and counter-claim arise out of the same set of facts.

[
2
]

The application at bar is a request by Blue
Mountain for security for costs under
s.236
of the
Business Corporations
Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c.57 (the “
Act
”).  Blue Mountain is
requesting that Scotford post security in the amount of $25,000.

[
3
]

The statement of claim was originally filed on
the 19
th
of September 2003 and an amended statement of claim was
filed on the 18
th
of May 2004.  When the litigation began there was
no such application to post security for costs.  It was only after counsel for
the defendant received a requirement to pay issued by Canada Customs and
Revenue Agency (hereinafter referred to as “CCRA”) some time after the 26
th

of November 2004 that the defendants turned their mind to the issue of security
for costs.  That requirement to pay suggested that Scotford had an unpaid
obligation to CCRA in the amount of $40,153.91.  It appears to be acknowledged
that since this requirement to pay was issued, Scotford has made arrangements
for payment of this obligation.  It is conceded that the obligation to CCRA arose
as a result of the dispute which forms the basis of this litigation.  It is
Scotford’s position that as they were not paid by Blue Mountain they could not
pay the required remittances to CCRA.

[
4
]

Prior to entering into a full discussion of the
law and the issues which need to be addressed in dealing with the defendant’s
application before the court, a summary of the parties’ respective positions is
appropriate.

II.         BLUE MOUNTAIN’S POSITION

[
5
]

Blue Mountain submits that the principles
guiding the use of discretion under
s. 236
of the
Act
suggest
that Blue Mountain need only show a
prima facie
case of the plaintiff
being unable to pay an award for costs against it.  The defendants argue that
where a company cannot satisfy its obligations to CCRA it is unlikely to meet
an award of costs against it, which makes out the
prima facie
case.
Further, Blue Mountain argues that the plaintiff does not have, on the basis of
financial disclosure made by the plaintiff to date, sufficient assets to meet a
cost award against it.  The disclosure by Scotford suggests a company with
slightly over $8,700 in accounts receivable and slightly over $5,300 in hard
assets.

[
6
]

Blue Mountain argues that the only basis for
which a court can refuse an order for security for costs is if the court were
to conclude that such an award would stifle the claim.  Blue Mountain states
that in order to defeat this application the plaintiff must demonstrate that it
would be unable to raise funds for security and the principal for Scotford, Mr.
Bedford, has declined to give any information on his assets or those of other
shareholders which could be used to fund security.  Finally, Blue Mountain
argues that the amount it claims as security for costs is reasonable in the
circumstance.

III.        SCOTFORD’S POSITION

[
7
]

Scotford agrees that the
prima facie
proof
of inability to pay is the first step.  Then, Scotford argues, the court is
required to determine whether such an award must be granted.  In making that
determination Scotford submits that the court may take into account the
defendant’s conduct.  They urge the court to consider that the alleged
impecuniosity in fact arises from the conduct of Blue Mountain.  Finally, Scotford
argues that should the court find that an order for security for costs is
warranted, it should be reasonable in the circumstances.

[
8
]

On the facts, Scotford argues that the defendant
has failed to make out the case for impecuniosity and secondly the defendant’s
conduct has caused the condition which gives rise to the concern about the plaintiff’s
ability to pay, and that should be taken into account in deciding on whether or
not security should be ordered.  Scotford argues that the money owing to CCRA
results from unremitted source deductions that Scotford was expected to pay
from the accounts receivable owing from Blue Mountain.  Scotford takes the
position that that is the sole basis of Blue Mountain’s argument that the
plaintiff will be unable to pay.  They point out that the principals of
Scotford have made payment arrangements with CCRA, that they are an ongoing
business, that they have service agreements in play for at least the next six
months and they argue that based on the financial disclosure they have an
ability to pay the awarded costs if unsuccessful.  Finally they argue that it
is essentially inequitable for the defendant to place the plaintiff in its
current financial situation and then base a request for security for costs on
that situation.

IV.       THE ISSUES

[
9
]

The issues raised by both the defendant/applicant
and the plaintiff in argument can best be dealt with by answering the four
questions noted below:

1.         What is the test to be followed in determining whether to
award security for costs?

2.         What is the effect of the impecuniosity of the plaintiff
if it is alleged  to have been caused by the act of the defendant, and this act
is the subject matter of the litigation?

3.         What is the effect of a counter-claim brought by the
defendant who is seeking security for costs against the plaintiff as it relates
to that application for security for costs?

4.         What is the proper way to address the issue of the amount
of the security to be ordered?

V.        THE LAW

1.  The Test:

[
10
]

Section 236
of the
Act
reads as follows:

236
If a corporation is the
plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court, and if it appears
that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant if the
defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require security to be
given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal proceedings
until the security is given.

[
11
]

The leading case in this area, which sets out
general considerations, is
Kropp v. Somerset Bay
(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29
B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 (C.A.).

[
12
]

The test for security for costs is best
articulated in the case of
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4
th
) 266
(B.C.S.C.).  In this case the plaintiff sued the defendant in defamation.  The
defendants brought an application pursuant to what was then
s. 205
of the
Company
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c.62, to have the plaintiff post security.  The plaintiff
was an Ontario corporation in financial difficulty.

[
13
]

Romilly J. set out in ¶ 14 the following process
to be followed in an application under what is now
s. 236
of the
Act
:

14     Based then, on
the decision in
Kropp
, supra
as well as the decision of
Spencer J. in
Ruko
, supra
, the test to be applied on an
application for security for costs is as follows:

1. Does it appear that the plaintiff company
will be unable to pay the defendants' costs if the action fails?

2. If so, has the plaintiff shown that it has
exigible assets of sufficient value to satisfy an award of costs?

3. Is the court satisfied that the defendants
have an arguable defence to present?

4. Would an order for costs visit undue
hardship on the plaintiff such that it would prevent the plaintiff's case from
being heard?

[
14
]

The fourth question set out by Romilly J. is
where a court considers,
inter alia
, the possibility that a claim will
be stifled.  Romilly J. made the following points on this question at ¶’s  22-23:

22     To succeed in
showing that an order for security would stifle the action, the plaintiff must
show that it has insufficient assets and no means of raising money for
security:
Kropp
,
supra
. In the case at bar, there is
dearth evidence as to the financial state of affairs of the plaintiff. There is
also a dearth of evidence as to any access the plaintiff may have to resources.
Consequently, though it appears that the plaintiff may be unable to pay costs
of the action, it does not follow, in the absence of evidence, that such a
state of affairs would result in stifling the advancement of the plaintiff's
claim if costs were ordered to be secured.

23     In sum, on an
application for security for costs, once the defendants
have established a
prima facie
case that
the plaintiff lacks exigible assets, the plaintiff is required to respond with
evidence to establish either that it will be able to pay the defendants' costs,
that the defendants have no arguable case, or that an order for security will
stifle the action. These tests serve to balance the possible injustice of
stifling the corporate plaintiff's claim against the possible injustices of
exposing the defendants to a law suit where they could not recover their costs
if successful.

[
15
]

This court in a number of other decisions has
adopted this test:  see
Zymtech Development Inc. v. Sport Central
Enterprises Ltd.
,
2004 BCSC 309
, a decision of Master Bishop and
Scopeset
Technology Inc. v. Astaro Corp.
,
2004 BCSC 830
,  a decision of Barrow
J.  In
Scopeset
, Barrow J. referred to the first three elements
of the test as a precondition to the exercise of the discretion, and the fourth
as the court’s exercise of discretion.

2.  Plaintiff’s Impecuniosity Allegedly
Tied to the Actions of the Defendant:

[
16
]

In
Grant v. Henderson Development (Canada)
Ltd.
,
2003 BCSC 1473
, the defendant sought an order for security for
costs against three corporate plaintiffs.  Allan J., at ¶ 6, stated that once a
defendant made out a
prima facie
case that the plaintiff would not be
able to pay costs, the plaintiff must either show it has exigible assets
sufficient to pay costs or that equitable factors make an order for security
inappropriate.  At  ¶ 7 Allan J. states that one such equitable factor is
impecuniosity, where an order may stifle the claim and deprive the plaintiff of
their day in court.  At ¶ 11 Allan J. stated:

11     One of the
principals of Punto [one of the corporate plaintiffs] deposes that if he is
required to pay security for costs, he may not be able to continue with the
lawsuit. He says that his company has no assets because of the conduct of the
defendants.

After setting out
the seven principles for the awarding of security from
Kropp
,
Allan J. reached the following conclusion with respect to Punto, at ¶ 23:
“Punto is likely to be deterred from pursuing its claims against the defendants
if security is ordered against it; its impecuniosity is tied to its claims in
this action.”  No other reasons were given for declining to award security
against Punto.

[
17
]

In
Gold River Chinook Project Society v.
Bowater Pulp & Paper Canada Inc.
,
2002 BCSC 166
, Barrow J. indicated
that where a defendant’s action was the basis of the plaintiff’s claim and also
their impecuniosity, this could be a reason for declining to award security for
costs requested by that defendant.  However, the impugned action was not the
basis of the claim in
Gold River
.  At ¶’s 32 and 34 Barrow J.
stated:

32     In
Tour-Mate
,

supra
, the actions of the defendant that were said to have caused or
contributed to the plaintiff's impecuniosity were the subject matter of the
outstanding litigation. The issue, broadly stated, in
Tour-Mate

was whether the defendant was entitled, in law, to do what it did. In those
circumstances, the court held that the defendant's conduct was a basis for reducing
the amount of security ordered…

34     Unlike the
situation in
Tour-Mate
,
supra
, the defendant has not done
anything that it was not entitled to do. It is obvious that the defendant's
actions have exacerbated the plaintiff's financial circumstances but the
actions were not, on the evidence, taken for the purpose of hindering the
plaintiff's ability to prosecute this claim, nor were the actions themselves
actionable at the instance of the plaintiff. In these circumstances, they are
not, in my view, a basis upon which to reduce or decline an order for security
for costs.

[
18
]

In
Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc.
,

2001 BCSC 1208
, the plaintiff and defendant by counterclaim brought an
application that the defendant corporation post security for costs associated
with its counterclaim pursuant to
s. 205
of the
Company Act
.  The
plaintiff’s claim and the defendant’s counterclaim both arose out of a failed
business arrangement entered into between the parties for the marketing of
computer software.  At ¶’s 23-26 Joyce J. refers to the relationship between
the parties and the effect on an award for security as follows:

23     The defendants say that an order
requiring them to post security for costs will prevent them from pursuing their
claim. They also say that their impecuniosity is the

direct result of the actions of the defendants
by counterclaim for which they claim damages and other relief. Counsel for the
applicants submits that while the evidence establishes that the defendants
would be unable to satisfy a judgment, the defendants have not put forward
evidence that they lack the ability to borrow money to enable them to post
security. He submits the defendants' submission that they cannot raise the
funds to provide security is a bald assertion without a sufficient evidentiary
basis to support it.

24    Counsel
for the applicants refers to
Kropp
,
supra
, at 262 where
Finch J.A. stated:

To succeed in showing that an order for security
would stifle the action the plaintiff must do more than show that it has no
assets: see
Paul v. General Mangaplate Corp.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 7259 (ON CTGD)
,
27 O.R. (3d)
314 (Gen. Div.)
. The defendants have already made out a
prima facie
case
that the corporate plaintiff has insufficient assets to pay costs if
unsuccessful. Mr. Kropp's affidavit does not really add to that position and
establish that the corporate plaintiff is impecunious, in the sense of lacking
any means of raising money for security. I think the law requires him to do so.
As Megarry, V.C., said in
Pearson
, supra, at 535, the purpose of the
provision is to protect "the community against litigious abuses by
artificial persons manipulated by natural persons."

25     Mr. Kropp had merely stated that he did
not have the resources to deposit the amount of security sought by the
defendants. He provided no details as to his own or the corporate plaintiff's
lack of assets or ability to sell assets or borrow money. In my opinion, Mr.
Stevenson's affidavit, while not as full as it might be, contains more than a
bald assertion of lack of assets and lack of ability to borrow money to provide
security.

26     In
addition, if the defendants allegations are proven at trial, their
impecuniosity is directly related to the actions of the defendants by
counterclaim.

[
19
]

The relationship between the defendant’s
impecuniosity and the allegations were a factor in Joyce J.’s decision to not
award security for costs.

[
20
]

Finally, in
Apex Mountain Resort Ltd. v.
British Columbia
,
1998 CarswellBC 1758 (S.C.)
the plaintiffs claimed
that the defendant province failed to make good on promises that it would
ensure continued access to the plaintiffs’ resort development.  The defendant
brought an application that the plaintiffs post security for costs as the
plaintiffs were in serious financial difficulty.  The plaintiffs admitted they
would be unable to pay but resisted the award of security on the grounds that
it would stifle their claim, and that their impecuniosity was tied to the
action of the defendant.  On the second ground, which Bauman J. referred to as
the causation argument, the plaintiffs argued that their impecuniosity “ought
not to damn them because that economic reality ha[d] been precipitated by the
very acts that found the litigation.”  Bauman J. accepted this position,
relying on
Kropp
, and the decision of the English Court of Appeal
which it cites,
Keary Developments Ltd. v. Tarmac Construction Ltd.
,

[1995] 3 All E.R. 534
.  At ¶’s 28-30 Bauman J. stated:

28     A reading of
Kropp

and
Keary
makes it clear that the plaintiffs' submission on
this issue must prevail.

29     In
Kropp
,
Finch J.A. (at 315) specifically referred to the principles "as more fully
articulated and explained in
Keary
" as a useful guide in
British Columbia.

30     Looking at
Keary
,
then, we find this more complete exposition of principle 3 (at 540 of
Keary
):

The court must carry out a balancing exercise.
On the one hand it must weigh the injustice to the plaintiff if prevented from
pursuing a proper claim by an order for security. Against that, it must weigh
the injustice to the defendant if no security is ordered and at the trial the
plaintiff's claim fails and the defendant finds himself unable to recover from
the plaintiff the costs which have been incurred by him in his defence of the
claim.
The court will properly be concerned not to allow the power to order
security to be used as an instrument of oppression, such as by stifling a
genuine claim by an indigent company against a more prosperous company,
particularly when the failure to meet that claim might in itself have been a
material cause of the plaintiff's
impecuniosity

(see
Farrer v Lacy, Hartland & Co

(1885)
28 Ch D 482
at 485

per Bowen LJ). But it will also be concerned not to be so reluctant to order
security that it becomes a weapon whereby the impecunious company can use its
inability to pay costs as a means of putting unfair pressure on the more
prosperous company (see
Pearson v Naydler

[1977] 3 All ER 531
at
537,
[1977] 1 WLR 899
at 906)
. (emphasis added by Bauman J.)

[
21
]

Bauman J. reasoned though, at ¶ 48, that the
causation argument should go to a determination of the quantum of an award for
security, rather than a determination of whether to award security at all.

48     I turn to the
causation argument. Assuming, of course, that the plaintiffs' allegations are
subsequently established, and I make no comment on their merits at this time,
then such an argument has force. But I conceive that in the balancing process
ordained by
Kropp

and
Keary
, this
consideration, in the circumstances at bar, is more relevant in determining the
quantum of security rather than as a trump card in an all-or-nothing analysis
of the application.

[
22
]

Bauman J. decided that an award of $100,000 was
appropriate in the case, while the defendants had requested between $390,000
and $540,000, noting that the fifth principle in
Kropp
allows a
judge to award any amount up to the full amount claimed by way of security.

[
23
]

From the cases cited above I take the following
propositions.  First, where a plaintiff corporation’s impecuniosity and the
cause of action against the defendant are linked, the Court may take this into
account in deciding whether to exercise discretion to award security for costs
or in determining the amount of security to award.

[
24
]

Second, the cases differ on what effect the
relationship between impecuniosity and the cause of action should have on the
exercise of discretion.
Grant
,
Gold River
and
Gray

are authority for the proposition that where there is a link, the Court may
decline to award security.  However, in
Apex Mountain
Bauman J.
stated that a link should go to the quantum of security awarded, rather than
whether or not to award security at all.  Bauman J. did note that he was
commenting on the circumstances at bar in that case in coming to that
conclusion.

[
25
]

In
Gray
, which contains more extensive
reasons than
Gold River
or
Grant
, Joyce J. based
his decision not to award costs on the conclusion that the claim would be
stifled if security were ordered, the link between the defendants impecuniosity
and the plaintiffs action, and the fact that the plaintiff was bringing a
counterclaim based on the same dispute.  I note that the dispute in
Gray

arose out of a contract between the parties.

[
26
]

In
Apex Mountain
, the dispute was
based on the allegation that various ministers of the provincial government gave
assurances, which the plaintiffs relied on, that access to the resort owned by
the plaintiffs would be maintained.  There was no contract between the
parties.  The link between the action and impecuniosity was the only factor
that militated against awarding security as Bauman J. did not accept that the
claim would be stifled as the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that they could
not obtain additional funds to finance litigation.

[
27
]

The results reached in
Apex Mountain

and
Gray
are distinguishable.  There was a stronger incentive in
Gray

to decline to award security as the plaintiff could not afford to pay security
and there were more circumstances militating against awarding security, whereas
in
Apex Mountain
the plaintiff could raise security, and, aside from
a connection between the action and the plaintiffs impecuniosity, no other
factors militated against an award of security.

[
28
]

A third point is that the plaintiff must
demonstrate that there is no way that it can obtain funds to finance the
litigation.  While this is not directly related to any link between
impecuniosity and the action, it has been treated by the Court as a
precondition for declining an award of security for costs.  This is based on
the comments of Joyce J. in
Gray
where he noted at ¶
25
that the
evidence presented by the plaintiff by counterclaim was not extensive, but
sufficient to support a conclusion that the plaintiff by counterclaim could not
obtain additional funds to finance the litigation.  This comment was based on
Kropp
,
at p. 262, where Finch J.A. (as he then was) stated that a plaintiff must
demonstrate that they are impecunious in the sense of lacking any means of
raising money to provide security.

[
29
]

To summarize, a plaintiff must first demonstrate
that they have no way of raising funds to continue litigation if an award of
costs is made against them:  see
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
,
and
Gray
.  If this is done then a connection between
impecuniosity and the action may contribute to a finding that the order should
not be made:  see
Gray
.  If a plaintiff does not demonstrate that
they have no way of raising funds then a connection between impecuniosity and
action may be considered in setting the quantum of security ordered: see
Apex
Mountain
.

3.  The Effect of a Counterclaim:

[
30
]

In
Gray
, a second factor that
Joyce J. referred to in deciding not to award security for costs relating to
the defendant’s counterclaim was that the claim and counterclaim were
intertwined.  At ¶’s 27 and 29:

27     Turning to the question of prejudice or
injustice to the plaintiff if the order for security is denied, it appears to
me that he will incur substantially the same costs in any event through the
prosecution of his own claim. The defence of the counterclaim may add to the
costs to some extent, at least on the issue of quantum of damages, but
considering the commonality of the issues in the claim and counterclaim it does
not appear to me that the plaintiff's costs will be substantially lessened if
the counterclaim does not proceed.

…

29     In my opinion, the claim and
counterclaim are so intertwined that it would constitute an injustice to permit
the claim to proceed while stifling the ability of the defendants to pursue a
counterclaim is founded on the same facts upon which the defence is dependent.
While the claim and counterclaim clearly have some distinct features,
particularly with respect to the nature and quantum of damages, both
proceedings have their genesis in the same agreement and its termination. Both
proceedings depend on a determination of which of the two parties was at fault
in the termination of the agreement.

[
31
]

I note, without commenting further at this point,
that the roles are reversed in the case at bar, in that security is being
sought against the plaintiff, Scotford, rather than the plaintiff by
counterclaim, Blue Mountain.

[
32
]

Gray
is
support for the proposition that where there is a claim and a counterclaim that
are based on the same dispute, it could constitute an injustice to require one
party to post security and stay its action should it fail to do so, yet permit
at the same time the other party to continue litigating the dispute to its
potential benefit.  While the roles are reversed in the case at bar, this same
consideration would apply, if the defendant chose to pursue its counterclaim
notwithstanding the stay of the plaintiff’s action.

4.  What is the Proper Amount of
Security to Be Set:

[
33
]

The defendants have provided a bill of costs
which suggests that at scale 3 the costs reasonably recoverable by the
defendants in this action would total approximately $25,000.  The plaintiff
does not seriously dispute this amount.

[
34
]

As for the case law, in
Galaxy Sports Inc.
v. Umbro Holdings Ltd.
,
2004 BCCA 208
, the appellants, defendants in
the action, submitted that the chambers judge erred,
inter alia
, in
failing to order that a greater amount of security be posted.  In chambers,
Galaxy Sports Inc. had conceded that it was insolvent and had the onus of
establishing that an order for security for costs was not appropriate.  The
chambers judge found that the defendants were entitled to an award for security
of $75,000, but not in the full amount of $130,000, which they were seeking, as
granting such an award might halt litigation.  At ¶ 17 Prowse J.A. for the
court stated:

17     In my view, the
Kropp

decision
does not stand for the proposition that
full
security
for costs must be ordered where the company resisting the posting of security
fails to lead adequate evidence concerning its ability to obtain financial
assistance from third parties. Failure to lead such evidence may well result in
an order for security for costs, but the
amount
of security lies within
the discretion of the chambers judge to be exercised having regard to a variety
of considerations. Some of those considerations are set forth at para. 17 of
Kropp
…

[
35
]

The court found that the chambers judge had
considered all the relevant factors and was well placed to make the decision
that a large lump sum security award could halt the litigation.

[
36
]

In
542641 B.C. Ltd. v. Wright Parry Land
Surveying & Engineering Ltd.
,
2004 BCSC 211
, security of
approximately $187,000 was requested by four defendants.  The corporate
plaintiff was impecunious and the principal of the company stated he could
raise no more than $20,000 to post as security.

[
37
]

Master McCallum referred to
Kropp
,
listing the factors to consider in exercising discretion adopted by Finch J.A.
(as he then was) from
Keary
.  The fifth factor is that t
he court can order any amount of security up to the full
amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than nominal.

[
38
]

At ¶ 9 Master McCallum made the following
comments with respect to this factor.  He stated that “The amount [posted] must
be more than nominal which I take to mean nominal given the amount claimed by
the defendants.”  He agreed with the plaintiff that their claim would be
stifled if the full amount of security were ordered, but also stated that more
than $20,000 security would have to be posted to avoid pressuring the
defendants to settle the case.

[
39
]

In
Cambridge International Bank &
Trust Co. v. Burns

et al.

2002 BCSC 1623
, a number of defendants
sought security for costs from the plaintiff.  The plaintiff’s assets consisted
of $10,000 and a jeep.  One defendant sought security in the amount of $390,000
including disbursements and two other defendants jointly sought approximately
$75,000 including disbursements.  They were awarded $100,000 and $10,000
respectively.  In awarding these amounts Bauman J. stated at ¶ 52:

52     In setting the
amount of security, I am engaged in an exercise attempting "to balance
injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of oppression to
stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means
of putting unfair pressure on the defendant on the other." (
Kropp

at para.
17
).

[
40
]

I note that one defendant received less than 20%
of the security award sought and the others received less than15% of the award they
sought.

[
41
]

From all of the cases cited above I take the
following propositions.  First, there is no obligation to award the full amount
of security requested as noted in
Kropp
.  Second, nominal does
not refer to a fixed amount of money but rather must be determined in relation
to the amount of security requested by the defendants:  see
Wright Parry
.
Awards of 15% to 25% of the amount requested by defendants were not considered
nominal by the judges awarding them:  see
Wright Parry
and
Cambridge
International
.  Third, if a judge or master considers that an award in
the amount requested will halt litigation he or she may reduce the award given:
see
Galaxy Sports
.  Furthermore, the link between the cause of
action and the impecuniosity, if not used to decline the award of security, may
be used to reduce the award given:  see
Apex Mountain
.  Finally,
though this was not set out in any of the cases, it would not be improper to
take into account the presence of a counterclaim in setting the quantum of
security if a security award was in fact made.

VI.       CONCLUSIONS

[
42
]

Referring back to the test as set out by
Romilly J. in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
, it does appear
that the plaintiff company, in this case Scotford, will be unable to pay the
defendants’ costs if the action fails.  Though Scotford is an active, ongoing
business, the cash flow of Scotford is relatively nominal and the accounts
receivable of Scotford appears to be only $8,700.

[
43
]

As for the second aspect of the test, the
plaintiff has shown that it has hard assets slightly in access of $5,300 in
value.  These are not sufficient to meet the award of costs.

[
44
]

Thirdly, though it was not argued extensively, a
review of the pleadings suggest that the defendants have an arguable defence to
the action of the plaintiff.

[
45
]

The fourth aspect of the test requires an
analysis of whether or not an order of costs would visit undue hardship on the
plaintiff such that it would prevent the plaintiff’s case from being heard.
There is no evidence before the court on the materials provided by Scotford
that such undue hardship would be visited on the plaintiff if an order for
costs was made.  In fact, there is very little information as to the ability of
the principals of Scotford to raise funds to meet any security for costs order.

[
46
]

However, that is not the end of the analysis.
It is important to note that in satisfying the first aspect of the test,
recognizing the plaintiff’s apparent inability to pay costs, that the alleged
impecuniosity is related directly to the alleged actions of the defendant.
Certainly, as noted above, the evidence of impecuniosity in this case, the
indebtedness owing to CCRA, is directly related to the dispute between the
plaintiff and the defendant which gives rise to this litigation.  As noted
Bauman J. at paragraph 30 of
Apex Mountain
, in his quote from the

Keary
decision of the English Court of Appeal, and I quote:

The court will properly be
concerned not to allow the power to order security to be used as an instrument
of oppression, such as by stifling a genuine claim by an indigent company
against a more prosperous company, particularly when the failure to meet that
claim might in itself have been a material cause of the plaintiff's
impecuniosity.

[
47
]

As noted in these reasons, there is some
distinction between the analysis of Joyce J. in the
Gray
case and
Bauman J. in
Apex Mountain
.  The distinguishing factor between
Gray

and
Apex Mountain
, as it relates to these facts, is that
in
Gray
the court was satisfied on the evidence that an order for
security would stifle the litigation, based on the affidavit evidence by the
principals of the defendants.  In
Apex
, the court determined that
the plaintiff could raise security.  On these facts, the lack of evidence
provided by Scotford or its principals suggesting an inability to raise funds
causes me to prefer an
Apex

Mountain
analysis in
the case at bar.  In the absence of evidence supporting the position, I cannot
conclude that Scotford cannot raise security.  However, I should consider the
alleged impecuniosity being related to the dispute between the parties in the
amount of the security I award.

[
48
]

Finally, I must note in this case that there is
a counterclaim by Blue Mountain against Scotford.  An oppressive amount of
security would create a significant injustice if it could stifle the ability of
the plaintiff to prosecute its claim while leaving the defendants free to pursue
their counterclaim.

[
49
]

Dealing directly with the amount of security
requested, I note that the defendants request $25,000 in security.  I must
consider, as noted above, that the apparent impecuniosity of the plaintiff
relates to the dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant.  I must
consider additionally, as noted above, that the defendants have a counterclaim
and the plaintiff must not be unduly restricted by an award for security for
costs so as to stifle their ability to defend against the counterclaim.
Several cases noted, having considered the direction in
Kropp

that the amount posted must be more than nominal, have awarded security
significantly less than what was claimed:  see
Galaxy Sports
and
Cambridge
International
.

[
50
]

Given those considerations, I direct that
Scotford post security in the amount of $6,000, with $3,000 to be posted prior
to the pending Rule 18A application, and a further $3,000 to be posted prior to
any trial.

[
51
]

In regards to the costs of this application,
there has been mixed success and each party will bear their own costs.

“Master
J. Groves”
